analysis.one_liner: Bans natural gas price gouging by utility companies during federally declared disasters.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors and died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without a hearing or vote, sitting there from April 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: During a federally declared major disaster — and for one year after — the bill would make it illegal for a gas utility to charge prices the Federal Trade Commission finds unconscionably excessive, meaning prices that take unfair advantage of the disaster. The FTC, working with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, could bring civil cases with penalties up to triple the excess profits or $100 million, whichever is smaller, and would give priority to the biggest utilities — those selling more than $2 billion of gas a year. The Justice Department could also bring criminal cases with fines up to $500 million, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents. The bill does not override any state law.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that buy natural gas in counties covered by a federal disaster declaration, especially in California where PG&E serves millions of customers, would be shielded from price spikes that a utility piles on during and after a catastrophe. The bill gives the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general new ways to punish a utility that overcharges, with fines large enough to matter to a big company.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households buying natural gas in disaster areas

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for a utility to charge unconscionably excessive natural gas prices in any county under a federal major disaster declaration, for the disaster period plus one year.

Lets the FTC enforce the ban with civil penalties up to triple the profits gained or $100 million, and directs the FTC to give priority to utilities with more than $2 billion a year in U.S. natural gas sales — a category that includes PG&E, the bill's namesake target.
Allows the Justice Department to bring criminal actions with fines up to $500 million, and lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents over retail price gouging.
Explicitly does not preempt state law, so existing state price-gouging rules remain in place alongside the new federal ban.

analysis.who_pays: Natural gas utilities, above all PG&E, which would face civil penalties, criminal fines, and lawsuits from state attorneys general if they raised gas prices beyond what the FTC judges fair during a disaster. Utility shareholders would bear those penalties, and any legitimate cost increases a utility needed to recover during a disaster would face a new layer of federal review.

drawbacks.text: The civil penalty is capped at $100 million, a sum that may be small relative to the revenues of a utility the bill itself acknowledges is big enough to have more than $2 billion a year in gas sales, weakening deterrence.

The standard is open-ended: a violation exists only if the FTC determines a price is 'unconscionably excessive,' which leaves utilities and courts to argue over what counts, and could take enforcement agencies time to establish.

A good-faith objection to any disaster price ceiling is that allowing prices to rise is one way to pull in extra supply when demand spikes after a catastrophe; a ban shifts the burden of policing that tradeoff onto regulators rather than the market.

The bill adds federal enforcement on top of state utility regulation, which already sets gas rates in states like California through public utility commissions, creating overlapping reviews of the same prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a narrow, well-aimed consumer protection: it applies only during federally declared disasters, targets only natural gas pricing, and leaves state law untouched. The penalties are real but the $100 million civil cap is modest for a utility of PG&E's scale, and the vague 'unconscionably excessive' standard would need regulators to flesh out. On balance the benefits to consumers in disaster zones outweigh the compliance burden on utilities, though the bill would not have transformed utility pricing generally.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its energy subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Josh Harder introduced the bill on April 13, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On April 21, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy, Climate and Grid Security, where no further action was taken.
The bill attracted no cosponsors over its entire life.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Natural gas utilities — PG&E above all — are better off, because they kept operating under existing state rate regulation with no new federal disaster price-gouging penalties. Consumers in disaster-declared counties gained no new protection, and the FTC, DOJ, and state attorneys general gained no new enforcement tool.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Natural gas utilities and their shareholders

for.name: Josh Harder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban natural gas price gouging during federally declared disasters; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee she chaired never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two years it sat on the panel's desk.

against.name: Subcommittee on Energy, Climate and Grid Security
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 21, 2023, and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no Republican or other Democrat cosponsored the bill, so no chamber-level party positions are on record; the single sponsor was a Democrat and the bill sat untouched in the Republican-controlled Energy and Commerce Committee. [S4][S5]

industries.note: The bill would let the FTC and state attorneys general penalize a utility for charging unconscionably excessive gas prices during a federally declared disaster, with civil penalties up to triple excess profits or $100 million and criminal fines up to $500 million. Its enforcement priority for utilities with more than $2 billion in annual gas sales points directly at large companies like PG&E, whose extra charges in a disaster come out of customers' bills.
